purpose: Three independent batch runs show the planner's LLM variance is confined to the AUTO/SAMPLE boundary and never touches which items are escalated to a human or hard-blocked.
method: Compared batch runs by assessment_id (position in data/queue.jsonl, since ControlEvidence entries carry no id field -- see docs/demo-script-v3.md BUG-2), not just by route counts. Route membership per id was diffed across all three runs.

runs.label: no key, planner fail-closed (all evaluators forced)

auto_union_sample_82.note: 82 = 100 - 9 - 9. Which items land in AUTO vs SAMPLE moves between runs; the set of 82 that were NOT escalated or blocked does not.

why_the_boundary_moves: SAMPLE fires when route_item sees min_score < LOW_CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD (0.8) among the evaluators the planner selected. Planner selection differs run to run (LLM), so an item can pick up an extra evaluator that pulls its min_score below 0.8 -- moving it AUTO->SAMPLE or back. WARN/FAIL verdicts from individual evaluators don't depend on how many evaluators ran, so HUMAN_REVIEW and BLOCK membership is unaffected by planner variance.
conclusion: The planner's variance is structurally confined to a boundary between two release outcomes (auto vs sampled release), never to the escalate/block decision. This is empirical support -- discovered, not designed -- for the project's central claim that the LLM triages but never decides release.
